newsitem.title: UK: British watchdog warns of bank dangers to savers.
newsitem.headline: British watchdog warns of bank dangers to savers.

text.p: Britain's borrowers will pay more and savers will earn less as a result of some of the largest building societies becoming banks, the head of a leading consumer watchdog said on Wednesday.

"Once the current round of conversions is complete almost 80 percent of savings and mortgages will be in the hands of six or seven big banks. This has serious implications for competition in the UK," Sheila McKechnie, chief executive of the Consumers' Association told the building societies' annual meeting.
McKechnie told the Building Societies Association (BSA) that banks would dominate distribution channels in Britain and warned of a danger of a levelling of competition.

The mutual versus bank debate took centre stage at the BSA's meeting, with delegates trumpeting the advantages of the traditional lenders to home-owners retaining their mutual status, where they are owned by their savers and borrowers.

The Alliance & Leicester has already traded in its mutual status for a stock market flotation and a new life as a bank. Halifax is due to make its stock market debut at the beginning of June and will be followed by other former building societies such as Northern Rock and the Woolwich.
Bristol & West has also left the ranks as it is being taken over by Bank of Ireland, bringing the number of societies represented at the meeting down to 72 from 77.
McKechnie also said banks had not been able to cushion customers to the same extent as building societies from the economic cycle.
"The bank's lack of commitment to the savings market means they've had to struggle to attract retail savings to reach the optimum funding mix," she added.

The Consumer Association's magazine Which? found that on a range of core products such as savings accounts, TESSAS, mortgages and overdrafts, an individual would have been "better off over five years with a high street building society compared to a bank".
McKechnie also raised the question of branch closures, which she said was having an effect on communities and restricting access to large numbers of consumers.

While voicing her support for sticking to the concept of mutuality, she also warned the societies against diversification. They would have to maintain a balance between efficiency and making sure they continued to beat banks in their core product range.
